outline.description: This chapter sets the stage by introducing the rise of large foundation models and the prohibitive costs of training them from scratch. It establishes the need for Parameter-Efficient Finetuning (PEFT) and provides an overview of existing adaptation paradigms, setting up the motivation for Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT).
subtopics: The rise of large foundation models (e.g., ChatGPT, Stable Diffusion) and their growing parameter counts
The computational challenge of training models from scratch vs. adapting pretrained models
Overview of task adaptation methods: model finetuning, adapter tuning, and prompt tuning
Reparameterization-based finetuning: an introduction to LoRA and its low-rank structure
Introduction to Orthogonal Finetuning (OFT) as an alternative multiplicative approach

outline.description: This chapter dives into the mathematical foundation and motivation behind OFT. It explains how OFT preserves the relational information (pairwise angles) of weight matrices during finetuning, and details the original OFT formulation including its use of Cayley parameterization and block-diagonal structures.
subtopics: The principle of preserving pretraining knowledge in model finetuning
Motivation for orthogonal transformations: preserving pairwise angles between neurons
Mathematical formulation of OFT: forward pass modification and orthogonal matrix multiplication
Cayley parameterization for ensuring orthogonality ($\bm{R}=(\bm{I}+\bm{Q})(\bm{I}-\bm{Q})^{-1}$)
Block-diagonal OFT: introducing sparsity for parameter efficiency and its limitations
The inductive bias problem of block-diagonal structures and the need for dense orthogonal matrices

outline.chapter_title: An Information Transmission Perspective on Matrix Factorization
outline.description: To address the parameter inefficiency of dense orthogonal matrices, this chapter introduces a novel information transmission framework. It reframes the generation of a dense matrix via the multiplication of sparse matrices as an information routing problem on a grid-structured graph.
subtopics: Composing dense orthogonal matrices with a product of multiple sparse matrices
Formulating matrix factorization as an information transmission problem on a grid-structured graph
Interpreting matrix sparsity patterns as information flow between adjacent graph levels
Key desiderata for efficient factorization: dense connectivity and minimum free edges
Analyzing the orthogonality constraint within the context of graph edges and bijections
Evaluating the block-diagonal structure's failure to achieve dense connectivity in the graph framework

outline.description: This chapter introduces the core technical contribution of the paper: Butterfly Orthogonal Finetuning (BOFT). It draws inspiration from the Cooley-Tukey fast Fourier transform algorithm to efficiently achieve dense connectivity using butterfly structures.
subtopics: Inspiration from the Cooley-Tukey fast Fourier transform (FFT) and its efficient information exchange topology
Mathematical definition of the butterfly factor $\bm{B}^F(k)$ and the recursive butterfly matrix $\bm{B}(d)$
Defining the butterfly component $\tilde{\bm{B}}(d,k)$ and its block-diagonal nature
Ensuring orthogonality of butterfly components using Cayley transform and block-wise permutations
Generalization to block butterfly components $\tilde{\bm{B}}^b(d,k)$ for broader applicability

outline.description: This chapter formalizes the BOFT method, explaining how the butterfly parameterization is applied to the finetuning process. It details the forward pass, parameter counting, initialization strategies, and a specialized dropout mechanism.
subtopics: Formulating the BOFT forward pass with the product of multiple orthogonal butterfly components
BOFT($m$,$b$) notation and its relationship to the block size $b$ and number of components $m$
How BOFT subsumes OFT as a special case (e.g., BOFT(1,$b$) reduces to block-diagonal OFT)
Parameter efficiency analysis: achieving $\mathcal{O}(d\log d)$ parameters compared to OFT's $\mathcal{O}(d^2)$
Identity initialization for butterfly components to start with the exact pretrained model
Multiplicative Dropout: adapting dropout for multiplicative weight updates by replacing blocks with identity matrices

outline.chapter_title: Theoretical Insights and Properties of BOFT
outline.description: This chapter explores the theoretical advantages of BOFT, contrasting its expressivity and inductive biases with standard OFT. It discusses why the butterfly structure provides a smoother interpolation between expressivity and regularity.
subtopics: Simulating the expressivity of BOFT vs. OFT in approximating random dense orthogonal matrices
Theorem 1: Proof that BOFT is more expressive than OFT with the same block size
Kaleidoscope hierarchy: generalizing BOFT to represent the entire orthogonal group
Spectral properties: preservation of the spectral norm of pretrained weights for training stability
Orthogonal finetuning as learning a bilinear similarity matrix with strong regularity
Inductive bias and generalization: the implicit benefits of structured classic linear transforms

outline.description: This chapter covers the extensive empirical study conducted to validate BOFT as a generic model finetuning method. It highlights the application of BOFT across different modalities and model architectures, comparing its performance against state-of-the-art methods.
subtopics: Applying BOFT to large vision transformers (ViTs) for computer vision tasks
Adapting large language models (LLMs) for natural language processing tasks
Finetuning text-to-image diffusion models for controllable generation
Comparative performance analysis of BOFT against LoRA and standard OFT
Evaluating parameter-efficiency, generalization ability, and training stability across diverse downstream tasks

outline.description: The final chapter concludes the textbook by discussing the limitations of the proposed BOFT method. It also outlines promising future research directions enabled by the information transmission framework.
subtopics: Training runtime overhead: the computational cost of multiplying multiple sparse matrices during training
Zero inference latency: merging the learned orthogonal matrices back into the pretrained weights
Open questions regarding the optimality of butterfly networks for information transmission
Future inspiration from computer networking topologies to discover even more efficient network structures
